Basal Ganglia Spiking Tutorial

Author: Matthew J. Crossley

Last update: 24 April, 2026

Learning objectives

By the end of this tutorial you should be able to:

  • explain the qualitative role of the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways
  • describe how disinhibition changes thalamic and cortical activity in a simple spiking circuit
  • explain how a simple dopamine manipulation changes the balance between D1 and D2 pathways
  • connect circuit-level dynamics to modelling choices in your final project

Why this tutorial matters for the final project

The previous Izhikevich tutorial focused on the behaviour of a single neuron. Your final project asks you to use Izhikevich neurons inside a basal ganglia model.

Later in the semester, those basal ganglia models will also need to learn. That means you will eventually add synaptic plasticity and show how experience changes connection strengths over time. Before you can do that well, you need to understand what the circuit is already doing before learning happens.

This tutorial is the bridge. Instead of asking what one neuron does under current injection, you will ask what a small basal ganglia circuit does when pathway structure changes. In this tutorial, focus on the following questions:

  • identify the state variables
  • identify which populations excite, inhibit, or disinhibit other populations
  • identify where stimulus information enters the circuit
  • explain how pathway structure changes thalamic gating and motor output
  • think ahead to how learning might later change those same pathways over time

General instructions

  • This tutorial is cumulative. Each section starts from the previous circuit and adds one new idea.
  • Run each code block before changing anything.
  • When you make an edit, write a short explanation of what changed and why.
  • Focus on qualitative circuit logic rather than exact spike timing.
  • If you get stuck, compare the connectivity matrix with the pathway diagram you have in mind.
  • After attempting the tutorial, you can check your work here: basal_ganglia_spiking_tutorial_solutions.html

1. Common ingredients

First load the ingredients used throughout the tutorial. This section only defines constants, labels, and neuron parameters. The circuit logic itself comes next.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Simulation time step and duration
dt = 0.1
T = 3000
t = np.arange(0, T, dt)
n_steps = t.shape[0]

# Fixed seed so everyone sees the same traces
np.random.seed(0)

# Sensory input arrives as a square pulse
I_amp = 300
I_in = np.zeros(n_steps)
I_in[n_steps // 3:2 * n_steps // 3] = I_amp

# Integer labels make the connectivity matrix easier to read
ctx = 0
d1 = 1
d2 = 2
gpi = 3
gpe = 4
th = 5
stn = 6
pm = 7

# These names are used later when plotting traces
labels = {
    ctx: "Sensory Cortex",
    d1: "D1 Striatum",
    d2: "D2 Striatum",
    gpi: "GPi",
    gpe: "GPe",
    th: "Thalamus",
    stn: "STN",
    pm: "Motor Cortex",
}

# Izhikevich parameters in the order:
# [C, vr, vt, vpeak, a, b, c, d, k]
iz_params = np.array([
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
    [50, -80, -25, 40, 0.01, -20, -55, 150, 1.0],
    [50, -80, -25, 40, 0.01, -20, -55, 150, 1.0],
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
    [100, -60, -40, 35, 0.03, -2, -50, 100, 0.7],
])

n_cells = iz_params.shape[0]

# Baseline external drive to selected nuclei
E_base = np.array([0, 0, 0, 300, 260, 0, 0, 0], dtype=float)

# Synaptic conductance update parameters
psp_amp = 1000
psp_decay = 100

2. A note about loops and pathway diagrams

The classical picture of basal ganglia organization emphasizes closed cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops: cortex influences basal ganglia, basal ganglia influence thalamus, and thalamus projects back to related cortical territories.

More recent work suggests that both closed and open motifs can exist. Here you will work with an open-loop example:

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{basal ganglia} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

That means the stimulus enters through sensory cortex, and the output of interest is its effect on motor cortex.

Within that larger sensory-to-motor chain, you will compare three pathways:

Direct pathway

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{D1 striatum} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

Indirect pathway

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{D2 striatum} \rightarrow \text{GPe} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

Hyperdirect pathway

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{STN} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

You will often see the indirect pathway written as D2 -> GPe -> STN -> GPi. In this tutorial, start with the compressed functional version D2 -> GPe -> GPi and later add the explicit STN route separately.

3. Direct pathway only

Start with the simplest complete sensory-to-motor chain:

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{D1 striatum} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

The core logic of the direct pathway is disinhibition. D1 striatal activity inhibits GPi, GPi normally inhibits thalamus, and reducing GPi output allows thalamus to respond more strongly.

This section also highlights an important modelling issue. Basal ganglia output does not excite thalamus directly. It mostly gates thalamus by inhibiting it. So where does thalamic excitation come from? In real brains, thalamus receives excitatory influences from cortex, cerebellum, and brainstem systems. In this model, that is represented with a simplified stimulus-related excitatory term to thalamus.

Tasks

  1. Run the code and inspect the five traces.
  2. In the connectivity matrix, identify the excitatory and inhibitory projections.
  3. Explain why increased D1 activity can increase thalamic and motor cortical activity even though D1 itself is inhibitory.
  4. Change W[d1, gpi] from -150 to -80. What becomes weaker?
  5. Why is it reasonable for thalamus to receive excitatory support in this model even though the basal ganglia themselves are not an excitatory drive to thalamus?
W = np.zeros((n_cells, n_cells))
W[ctx, d1] = 250
W[d1, gpi] = -150
W[gpi, th] = -120
W[th, pm] = 120

v = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
u = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
g = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
spike = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))

v[:, 0] = iz_params[:, 1] + np.random.rand(n_cells) * 5
u[:, 0] = iz_params[:, 5] * (v[:, 0] - iz_params[:, 1])

for i in range(1, n_steps):
    dt = t[i] - t[i - 1]

    I_net = W.T @ g[:, i - 1]
    I_net[ctx] += I_in[i - 1]
    I_net[th] += I_in[i - 1]
    I_net += E_base

    for j in range(n_cells):
        C, vr, vt, vpeak, a, b, c, d, k = iz_params[j]

        dvdt = (k * (v[j, i - 1] - vr) * (v[j, i - 1] - vt) - u[j, i - 1] + I_net[j]) / C
        dudt = a * (b * (v[j, i - 1] - vr) - u[j, i - 1])
        dgdt = (-g[j, i - 1] + psp_amp * spike[j, i - 1]) / psp_decay

        v[j, i] = v[j, i - 1] + dvdt * dt
        u[j, i] = u[j, i - 1] + dudt * dt
        g[j, i] = g[j, i - 1] + dgdt * dt

        if v[j, i] >= vpeak:
            v[j, i - 1] = vpeak
            v[j, i] = c
            u[j, i] += d
            spike[j, i] = 1

plot_cells = [ctx, d1, gpi, th, pm]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(len(plot_cells), 1, squeeze=False, figsize=(8.5, 7.2), sharex=True)
fig.suptitle("Direct Pathway Only")

for row, cell_idx in enumerate(plot_cells):
    ax1 = ax[row, 0]
    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    ax1.plot(t, v[cell_idx, :], color="C0", alpha=0.25)
    ax2.plot(t, g[cell_idx, :], color="C1", alpha=1.0, linewidth=2.0)
    ax1.set_ylabel(labels[cell_idx], fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Think

Describe the sign of each link in the chain from ctx to pm. Which step implements disinhibition?

4. A small helper

You have now seen the full simulation loop once. From this point on, the same logic is wrapped in a helper function so that you can focus on pathway changes rather than rewriting the whole Euler loop every time.

def simulate_network(W, E):
    v = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
    u = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
    g = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))
    spike = np.zeros((n_cells, n_steps))

    v[:, 0] = iz_params[:, 1] + np.random.rand(n_cells) * 5
    u[:, 0] = iz_params[:, 5] * (v[:, 0] - iz_params[:, 1])

    for i in range(1, n_steps):
        dt = t[i] - t[i - 1]

        I_net = W.T @ g[:, i - 1]
        I_net[ctx] += I_in[i - 1]
        I_net[th] += I_in[i - 1]
        I_net += E

        for j in range(n_cells):
            C, vr, vt, vpeak, a, b, c, d, k = iz_params[j]

            dvdt = (k * (v[j, i - 1] - vr) * (v[j, i - 1] - vt) - u[j, i - 1] + I_net[j]) / C
            dudt = a * (b * (v[j, i - 1] - vr) - u[j, i - 1])
            dgdt = (-g[j, i - 1] + psp_amp * spike[j, i - 1]) / psp_decay

            v[j, i] = v[j, i - 1] + dvdt * dt
            u[j, i] = u[j, i - 1] + dudt * dt
            g[j, i] = g[j, i - 1] + dgdt * dt

            if v[j, i] >= vpeak:
                v[j, i - 1] = vpeak
                v[j, i] = c
                u[j, i] += d
                spike[j, i] = 1

    return v, g, spike


def plot_pathway_columns(
    v,
    g,
    columns,
    title
):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(
        5,
        len(columns),
        squeeze=False,
        figsize=(10.5, 7.8),
        sharex=True
    )
    fig.suptitle(title)

    for col, (column_title, cell_list) in enumerate(columns):
        for row, cell_idx in enumerate(cell_list):
            ax1 = ax[row, col]
            if cell_idx is None:
                ax1.axis("off")
                continue
            ax2 = ax1.twinx()
            ax1.plot(t, v[cell_idx, :], color="C0", alpha=0.25)
            ax2.plot(
                t,
                g[cell_idx, :],
                color="C1",
                alpha=1.0,
                linewidth=2.0
            )
            if row == 0:
                ax1.set_title(column_title)
            ax1.set_ylabel(labels[cell_idx], fontsize=8)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

5. Add the indirect pathway

Now add a second route from cortex through D2 striatum and GPe.

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{D2 striatum} \rightarrow \text{GPe} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

The usual textbook shorthand is that the direct pathway is a go pathway and the indirect pathway is a no-go pathway. That language is oversimplified, but it is still useful at this stage if you treat it as a statement about net gating tendency:

  • stronger direct pathway tends to facilitate thalamocortical output
  • stronger indirect pathway tends to suppress thalamocortical output

Tasks

  1. Run the code and identify the three connections that implement the indirect pathway.
  2. Run the simulation and compare it with the direct-only case.
  3. Explain why inhibiting GPe can increase GPi output.
  4. Increase the magnitude of the D2 to GPe inhibition and describe the qualitative effect on thalamus.
  5. Make the direct pathway stronger than the indirect pathway and describe the result.
  6. Make the indirect pathway stronger than the direct pathway and describe the result.
  7. You will often see the indirect pathway written as D2 -> GPe -> STN -> GPi. Why can the compressed version used here still capture a similar functional effect on GPi and thalamus?
W = np.zeros((n_cells, n_cells))

# direct pathway
W[ctx, d1] = 250
W[d1, gpi] = -150

# indirect pathway
W[ctx, d2] = 250
W[d2, gpe] = -120
W[gpe, gpi] = -40

# output
W[gpi, th] = -120
W[th, pm] = 120

v, g, spike = simulate_network(W, E_base)
columns = [
    ("Direct", [ctx, d1, gpi, th, pm]),
    ("Indirect", [None, d2, gpe, None, None]),
]
plot_pathway_columns(v, g, columns, "Direct + Indirect Pathways")

Think

Why does adding a second inhibitory step sometimes produce a net increase in GPi output rather than a decrease? In your own words, why can the indirect pathway act like a no-go pathway?

6. Add the hyperdirect pathway

Now add a fast excitatory projection from cortex to STN and then from STN to GPi.

\[ \text{Sensory cortex} \rightarrow \text{STN} \rightarrow \text{GPi} \rightarrow \text{thalamus} \rightarrow \text{motor cortex} \]

The key teaching idea is that the same cortical event can now push GPi in opposite directions through different routes:

  • direct pathway tends to reduce GPi output
  • hyperdirect pathway tends to increase GPi output

Like the indirect pathway, the hyperdirect pathway is often treated as a no-go route. The important difference is speed. Hyperdirect reaches GPi through fewer intermediate steps, so it can suppress thalamocortical output more quickly.

Tasks

  1. Add the hyperdirect weights.
  2. Run the simulation and compare GPi activity with the previous section.
  3. Explain why the hyperdirect pathway is often described as fast global suppression.
  4. Reduce W[ctx, stn] by half and describe what changes.
  5. Whay is the hyperdirect pathway adding beyond what the indirect pathway already does?
W = np.zeros((n_cells, n_cells))

# direct pathway
W[ctx, d1] = 250
W[d1, gpi] = -150

# indirect pathway
W[ctx, d2] = 250
W[d2, gpe] = -120
W[gpe, gpi] = -40

# hyperdirect pathway
W[ctx, stn] = 100
W[stn, gpi] = 50

# output
W[gpi, th] = -120
W[th, pm] = 120

v, g, spike = simulate_network(W, E_base)
columns = [
    ("Direct", [ctx, d1, gpi, th, pm]),
    ("Indirect", [None, d2, gpe, None, None]),
    ("Hyperdirect", [None, stn, None, None, None]),
]
plot_pathway_columns(v, g, columns, "Direct + Indirect + Hyperdirect Pathways")

Think

If direct and hyperdirect pathways are both driven by sensory cortex, why do they not do the same thing to GPi? When you compare direct + indirect with direct + hyperdirect, what looks faster?

7. Dopamine modulation

Now keep the pathway structure in place and change dopamine tone.

In this simplified model, dopamine scales corticostriatal efficacy in opposite directions:

  • higher dopamine strengthens ctx -> d1
  • higher dopamine weakens ctx -> d2

This is deliberately simple, but it captures the idea that dopamine can bias the balance between pathways.

Tasks

  1. Run the three dopamine conditions.
  2. Compare D1, D2, GPi, thalamus, and motor cortex across conditions.
  3. Explain why increasing dopamine in this model tends to favour movement facilitation.
  4. Change k_da from 0.6 to 0.3. What becomes less extreme?
W_base = np.zeros((n_cells, n_cells))

# direct pathway
W_base[ctx, d1] = 250
W_base[d1, gpi] = -150

# indirect pathway
W_base[ctx, d2] = 250
W_base[d2, gpe] = -120
W_base[gpe, gpi] = -40

# hyperdirect pathway
W_base[ctx, stn] = 100
W_base[stn, gpi] = 50

# additional recurrent connectivity
W_base[stn, gpe] = 20
W_base[gpe, stn] = -50

# output
W_base[gpi, th] = -120
W_base[th, pm] = 120

da_conditions = [
    ("Low DA", -0.5),
    ("Baseline DA", 0.0),
    ("High DA", 0.5),
]
k_da = 0.6

da_results = []
for da_label, da_level in da_conditions:
    W = W_base.copy()
    d1_scale = max(0.0, 1 + k_da * da_level)
    d2_scale = max(0.0, 1 - k_da * da_level)
    W[ctx, d1] = W_base[ctx, d1] * d1_scale
    W[ctx, d2] = W_base[ctx, d2] * d2_scale
    v, g, spike = simulate_network(W, E_base)
    da_results.append((da_label, v, g))

columns = [
    ("Direct", [ctx, d1, gpi, th, pm]),
    ("Indirect", [None, d2, gpe, None, None]),
    ("Hyperdirect", [None, stn, None, None, None]),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(5, len(columns), squeeze=False, figsize=(10.5, 7.8), sharex=True)
fig.suptitle("Dopamine Modulation: Output Comparison")

colors = {
    "Low DA": "tab:red",
    "Baseline DA": "black",
    "High DA": "tab:blue",
}

for col, (column_title, cell_list) in enumerate(columns):
    for row, cell_idx in enumerate(cell_list):
        ax1 = ax[row, col]
        if cell_idx is None:
            _ = ax1.axis("off")
            continue
        for da_label, v, g in da_results:
            _ = ax1.plot(t, g[cell_idx, :], color=colors[da_label], linewidth=2.0, label=da_label)
        if row == 0:
            _ = ax1.set_title(column_title)
        _ = ax1.set_ylabel(labels[cell_idx], fontsize=8)
        if row == 0 and col == 0:
            _ = ax1.legend(loc="upper right")

_ = plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Think

Why does this model treat dopamine as a change in pathway balance rather than as a generic increase in activity everywhere?
